title: Joseph Swan Lights Up Newcastle
summary: Joseph Swan was a chemist in Newcastle, England, who spent years baking strips of paper and thread into carbon and sealing them in glass. In 1879 he showed hundreds of people a glowing lamp with no flame at all. Soon his bulbs lit his own house, a castle-like mansion powered by lakes, and a whole London theatre.

sections.heading: A Chemist's Boy from Sunderland
paragraphs: On 31 October 1828, in a house called Pallion Hall near the River Wear in Sunderland, in the north-east of England, a baby named Joseph Wilson Swan was born. Sunderland was a town of shipyards, coal and busy quays. Smoke from chimneys and ships hung over the river, and at night the streets were lit by flickering gas lamps and the windows of homes by candles and oil. Nobody in that town, and nobody anywhere in the world, had ever seen a room lit by a glowing electric bulb. Before Joseph Swan died, millions of people would have.

Young Joseph was curious about everything. He liked machines, he liked chemistry, and he loved reading about the experiments of scientists such as Humphry Davy and Michael Faraday, whose discoveries you met in earlier parts of this story. When he was a teenager he was apprenticed for six years to a firm of pharmacists in Sunderland called Hudson and Osbaldiston. An apprentice was a young worker who learned a trade by helping an expert, a bit like a very long work-experience placement. In a pharmacy, Swan learned how to weigh chemicals carefully, mix solutions, heat substances in flasks and keep a tidy, safe workbench. These were exactly the skills an inventor would need later.

In 1846 Swan moved a few miles north to Newcastle upon Tyne to join the chemist's business of his brother-in-law, John Mawson. Mawson's shop is said to have been founded in 1828, the same year Swan was born. Swan soon became a partner, and the firm later traded under the name Mawson, Swan and Morgan. It sold medicines, chemicals and, increasingly, supplies for the exciting new hobby of photography.

Newcastle in the middle of the 1800s was one of the most inventive cities on Earth. Coal from the surrounding mines was shipped down the River Tyne to London and around the world. George and Robert Stephenson had built famous locomotives nearby. The engineer William Armstrong ran enormous works on the riverbank that made cranes, hydraulic machines and, later, ships and guns. The city also had a remarkable club for curious minds: the Literary and Philosophical Society of Newcastle upon Tyne, usually called the Lit and Phil, founded in 1793 as a 'conversation club'. Its members met in a handsome library on Westgate Road to hear lectures and argue about the latest science. Armstrong was its president for forty years, from 1860 to 1900, and Swan was an enthusiastic member.

So picture the scene: a young chemist with steady hands, a shop full of chemicals, a city full of engineers and a society full of people who loved new ideas. It was the perfect place for someone to take on one of the hardest puzzles of the age: how to make electricity give a gentle, steady light that could be used inside a home.

sections.heading: Paper in a Glass Bubble
paragraphs: Swan started working on electric light in about 1850, when he was only around 22 years old. He knew the basic idea that you read about in Part 8: if you push enough electric current through a thin strip of material, it heats up, and if it gets hot enough it glows. This glowing-from-heat is called incandescence. The challenge was finding a strip, which inventors called a filament, that could glow brightly for hours without melting, breaking or burning away.

Swan chose carbon. Carbon is the black stuff in soot, charcoal and pencil 'lead' (which is really graphite, a form of carbon). It has a huge advantage: it does not melt at ordinary furnace temperatures. Instead, if it gets extremely hot it turns straight into vapour, and that only happens at temperatures well above 3,000 degrees Celsius. That meant a carbon filament could, in theory, glow white-hot without dripping like a metal wire might.

But how do you make a thin strip of carbon? Swan's trick was to start with something that was already thin and flexible, such as paper or card, and bake it. He cut strips of paper, packed them in powdered charcoal inside a closed container so that air could not get at them, and heated them in a fire. The heat drove off everything in the paper except the carbon, leaving a fragile black skeleton of the original strip. This process is called carbonising. If you have ever seen a piece of toast that was left far too long under the grill and turned black right through, you have seen a rough kind of carbonising.

There was a big catch. Carbon burns in air. If you heat a carbon strip to glowing in an ordinary room, the oxygen in the air reacts with it and it burns away in moments, just like a piece of charcoal on a barbecue. So Swan sealed his carbon strips inside glass bulbs and pumped out as much air as he could, trying to create a vacuum, an empty space with almost no gas inside.

By about 1860 Swan had a lamp that actually worked. It glowed. But it did not glow for long. The pumps of the day could not remove enough air, so the few oxygen molecules left inside slowly attacked the filament. The batteries that supplied the electricity were expensive, weak and messy, and there were not yet any good dynamos to make current from motion. Swan's lamps were short-lived and inefficient, and he could not see a way to make them practical.

So he put the problem aside, though he never really forgot it. For the next fifteen years he poured his energy into photography instead, where he made important inventions that we will come back to at the end of this part. It is worth remembering that this was not giving up. Sometimes an idea is simply ahead of the tools needed to make it work, and a wise inventor waits until the tools catch up.

sections.heading: Better Pumps and a Night in Newcastle
paragraphs: The tool that finally caught up was the vacuum pump. In 1865 the German-born chemist Hermann Sprengel, working in London, invented a pump that used falling drops of mercury to trap tiny pockets of air and carry them away, little by little, out of a glass vessel. You read about it in Part 8. Sprengel's pump was slow, but it could make a far emptier space than older piston pumps. (According to some accounts, Swan himself had described a mercury pump design to the British Association in 1863, a couple of years before Sprengel's work, but it was the Sprengel pump that became widely used.)

In about 1875 Swan returned to his old dream. This time he had an important helper: Charles Stearn, a skilled experimenter with vacuum pumps. Together they tackled the problem that had always killed early lamps. Even in a good vacuum, a new carbon filament would give off gases trapped inside it when it first heated up, and soot-like carbon would drift off and coat the inside of the glass. The bulb went black and dim, and the filament wore away.

Swan and Stearn worked out a clever answer. They kept pumping air out of the bulb while current was already flowing through the filament and making it hot. The heat drove out the hidden gases, and the pump carried them away before the bulb was sealed. The result was a cleaner vacuum and a filament that did not ruin its own glass so quickly. Swan later received a British patent for this processing method in 1880.

Now the story arrives at a famous evening. On 18 December 1878 Swan gave a talk to the Newcastle Chemical Society and showed a carbon lamp glowing inside its glass bulb. This was his first public demonstration of the new lamp. According to accounts of the meeting, the demonstration did not go perfectly: the lamp was given too much current and failed. Even so, the idea had been shown in public, and Swan repeated the lecture successfully on 17 January 1879.

Then came the big show. On 3 February 1879 Swan spoke at the Lit and Phil in Newcastle, with his friend William Armstrong in the chair. More than 700 people squeezed in to listen. Imagine the hall, normally lit by gas, with its rows of eager faces, and the quiet moment when Swan connected his apparatus and a small, steady, smokeless glow appeared inside a glass bubble. There was no flame, no smell and no flicker. For many people in that room, it was the first electric light they had ever seen that was not a blinding, sputtering arc lamp.

It is important to be fair here. The lamps Swan showed in 1878 and 1879 were not yet a finished product. Their filaments were fairly thick carbon rods, and they did not last very long. They proved the idea, but they had a hidden weakness that you will meet in the next section. Still, these Newcastle demonstrations came months before Thomas Edison's team in America had its first long-lasting carbon lamp, which is why historians say Swan and Edison were racing side by side, not one behind the other.

sections.heading: Thick Rods, Thin Threads
paragraphs: To understand Swan's hidden weakness, we need a quick bit of electrical science. Every material holds back electric current a little. This holding-back is called resistance, measured in ohms. A thick, short piece of carbon has low resistance: current flows through it easily. A long, very thin thread of carbon has high resistance: current has to squeeze through it.

Swan's early rods were fairly thick, so they had low resistance. To make a low-resistance filament glow white-hot, you need to push a large current through it. Large currents cause a problem in the wires that bring the electricity to the lamp. Wires heat up and waste energy when they carry big currents, and the waste grows very fast: double the current and you get about four times as much heating in the wire. To carry big currents without huge losses, you need very thick copper cables, and copper is expensive. Lighting a whole street of houses this way would have meant laying a fortune in copper under the pavement.

There was a second issue. Low-resistance lamps worked best when they were connected in series, one after another in a single loop, like beads on a necklace. The trouble with a series loop is that if one lamp breaks, the loop is broken and every lamp goes out, and you cannot easily switch one room off without affecting the others. For homes, it is much better to connect lamps in parallel, where each lamp has its own path from the main wires, so each can be switched on or off by itself. Parallel lighting on a big scale works best with high-resistance lamps that each take only a small current. This is the very idea that Edison's team concentrated on, as you will see in Part 10.

Swan realised his filament needed to be thinner and tougher. His answer came from chemistry. He took ordinary cotton thread and soaked it in sulfuric acid, which changed the surface of the cotton into a smooth, tough, almost horn-like material. This was called 'parchmentised' thread, because a similar acid treatment was used to make strong parchment paper. When the treated thread was carbonised, it gave a thin, even, springy carbon filament that was far better than his old rods. Swan received British patent number 4933 for this on 27 November 1880.

He kept improving. In 1881 Swan patented a process for squeezing a syrupy form of cellulose, called nitrocellulose, through tiny holes to make long, perfectly even threads. Cellulose is the natural material that makes up plant fibres like cotton and wood. These man-made threads could be carbonised into very uniform filaments, and over the next decades squirted-cellulose filaments became the standard way to make carbon lamps. Interestingly, the same idea of pushing a liquid through tiny holes to make fibres was later taken up by the textile industry, helping lead to artificial silks. Swan's lamp research had accidentally helped invent a new kind of thread for clothes.

By 20 October 1880 Swan's improved lamps were good enough to light the lecture room of the Lit and Phil during a talk, and the society proudly describes its building as the first public building lit this way. The gentle glow had moved out of the laboratory and into a room full of ordinary people.

sections.heading: Underhill and the Wizard's Castle
paragraphs: Swan did much of his experimenting at home, in the conservatory of his house called Underhill, at Low Fell in Gateshead, just across the River Tyne from Newcastle. A conservatory is a glass room attached to a house, usually full of plants, and Swan's was full of glassware, batteries and wires instead. Underhill is often described as the first house in the world to be lit by working electric light bulbs. Today a blue plaque marks the spot. Imagine being one of Swan's children, walking into a room in the evening and seeing it filled with steady light from little glass globes, while every other house in the street still glowed orange with gas and candles.

The next house to shine belonged to Swan's friend William Armstrong. Armstrong was a lawyer who had become one of Britain's greatest engineers. He had built a country house called Cragside, perched on a rocky hillside above the Debdon Burn near Rothbury in Northumberland. Armstrong loved water power. He built dams on his estate to create five new lakes, and used the falling water to drive machines.

In 1870 Armstrong had a water-powered engine on the estate drive a Siemens dynamo, and by 1878 this was lighting an arc lamp in Cragside's picture gallery. This made Cragside a pioneer of hydroelectric power: electricity made from moving water. But as you read in Part 7, an arc lamp is a harsh, dazzling thing, more suited to a street than a room full of paintings.

In 1880 Swan personally supervised the fitting of his incandescent lamps at Cragside. The gallery got twelve overhead lamps, with eight more that could be switched on using current borrowed from the dining room lamps when nobody was eating. Swan called it 'the first proper installation' of his lighting. It was the first private home, other than Swan's own, to be lit by his bulbs, and it was powered not by coal but by water from Armstrong's lakes, sent through a generator in a building later known as the Burnfoot Power House. Today Cragside is looked after by the National Trust, and a modern water turbine installed in 2014 once again makes some of the house's electricity.

Swan lamps soon spread far beyond Northumberland. In June 1881 the passenger steamship City of Richmond was fitted with them, and the Royal Navy started using them too, with the warship HMS Inflexible among the first. On a ship, a flame-free light was a huge safety improvement. Swan also helped develop electric safety lamps for coal miners, shown in Newcastle in 1881. In mines, an open flame could set off an explosion of the gas called firedamp, so a light with its glowing part sealed inside glass was a very attractive idea. In 1881 Swan founded the Swan Electric Light Company to make lamps in large numbers, and later that year his lamps were shown at the great International Exposition of Electricity in Paris, where he won a French honour, the Legion of Honour.

sections.heading: The Savoy: A Theatre Without Gas
paragraphs: The most famous early Swan installation was in London. Richard D'Oyly Carte was a theatre producer who presented the comic operas of W. S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan, such as The Pirates of Penzance. Their shows were so popular that Carte built a brand-new theatre for them beside the Strand in London, called the Savoy. It opened on 10 October 1881 with Gilbert and Sullivan's opera Patience, which moved there from another theatre where it had been running since April.

Victorian theatres were lit by hundreds of gas jets. They were hot, they used up oxygen, and they left the air stuffy and smelly. Worse, theatres were full of painted scenery, curtains and costumes, and gas-lit theatre fires were a terrible danger in the 1800s. Carte decided to do something nobody had done before: light an entire public building with electricity. He argued that electric lamps did not make the air hot and stuffy like gas, and that they 'consume no oxygen'.

Swan supplied about 1,200 of his lamps. Electricity came from a 120-horsepower steam-driven generator set up on open land near the theatre. At first the generator was not big enough for everything, so the auditorium and front of house were lit electrically while the stage was still lit by gas. On 28 December 1881 the stage was switched over too, and from then on the Savoy was lit entirely by electricity, making it the first public building in the world to be so. Gas lights were kept as a backup, but they were rarely needed.

Many people in the audience were nervous. Wasn't electricity the stuff of lightning? Might the lamps explode or start a fire? Carte answered with a piece of showmanship. On stage, in front of the audience, he took a glowing lamp and broke it. The light went out, and nothing caught fire. A gas jet would never have been so harmless. The message was clear: this new light was safe.

Newspapers were impressed. The Times judged that the electric light was clearly better than gaslight for seeing the stage. Audiences could see the actors' faces more clearly, the colours of costumes looked truer, and the hall stayed cooler. Today a plaque at the Savoy remembers Swan's achievement. A London theatre audience laughing at a comic opera might not seem like a turning point in history, but for many wealthy Londoners the Savoy was the place where they first saw electric light behave like a friendly servant instead of a dangerous wild animal.

sections.heading: Rivals Become Partners
paragraphs: While Swan was lighting Newcastle, Gateshead and London, Thomas Edison's team in New Jersey was racing toward the same goal. Edison had boldly told reporters he would solve electric lighting, and in January 1880 he received his American patent for a carbon-filament lamp. Both men developed their lamps independently, and both patented them around 1880. Each had good reason to think the bulb was his.

When Edison's company began selling lamps in Britain, a clash was almost certain. Swan held strong British patents, and he had shown working carbon lamps in public in Newcastle before Edison's famous demonstrations. Edison held patents too. Accounts differ about exactly who sued whom and in what order, but it is clear that both sides started legal action over their patents, and that a long fight in court would have been costly and uncertain for both. Swan's early public demonstrations made it very hard for Edison to claim that the whole invention was his alone in Britain.

So, instead of fighting to the end, the two sides made a deal. In 1883 the Swan and Edison businesses in Britain merged to form the Edison and Swan United Electric Light Company. People quickly shortened the long name to 'Ediswan', and Ediswan lamps became famous across the British Empire. The company made its lamps at a factory at Ponders End in north London, and later it made radio valves there too: glass tubes that grew out of light bulb technology and powered early radios.

The story of Swan and Edison is a good lesson in how invention really works. It was not one lonely genius suddenly shouting 'Eureka!' It was a crowd of people across several countries, building on Davy, de Moleyns, Sprengel and many others, and sometimes arriving at similar answers at almost the same time. In Britain, Swan's name is often given first place. In America, Edison's is. A fair historian gives both their due: Swan for his early, practical carbon lamps and lovely lighting installations, and Edison's team for a long-lasting lamp and a whole electrical system to run it.

sections.heading: Pictures, Honours and a Long Life
paragraphs: Swan's light bulb was not his only great invention. During the years when he had put electric light aside, he became one of the most important figures in early photography. In 1864 he patented the carbon process, a way of making photographic prints using a pigment such as carbon in gelatine. Carbon prints did not fade the way many early photographs did, and Swan sold his patents for the process to the Autotype Company in 1868.

He also noticed that gently heating a type of light-sensitive emulsion made with silver bromide made it far more sensitive to light. This helped lead to faster 'dry plates', which photographers could buy ready-made instead of having to coat glass plates with wet chemicals moments before taking a picture. Then, in 1879, the same year as his famous light bulb lecture, he patented bromide paper. This was paper coated with a silver bromide emulsion, and it became the standard paper for printing black-and-white photographs for many decades. If you have ever seen an old family photo from the 1900s, there is a good chance it was printed on a descendant of Swan's bromide paper.

Swan's family life had sadness as well as joy. He married Frances White, known as Fanny, in 1862, and after her death in 1868 he married her younger sister, Hannah, in 1871. He had several children. His daughter Frances Isobel became a sculptor. Her son, Christopher Morcom, was a close school friend of the future computer pioneer Alan Turing.

Honours piled up. Swan was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society, Britain's leading science academy, in 1894. He became president of the Institution of Electrical Engineers in 1898, and in 1903 he was the first president of the Faraday Society, named after the hero whose lectures he had read about as a boy. In 1904 King Edward VII knighted him, so he became Sir Joseph Swan, and in the same year the Royal Society awarded him its Hughes Medal. He died at his home in Warlingham, Surrey, on 27 May 1914, aged 85, having lived from the age of candles and gas into an age when electric light was spreading through cities across the world.

But to see how electric light became an entire industry, we have to cross the Atlantic Ocean. In a small village in New Jersey, in a long white wooden building full of bottles, wires and machines, a famous inventor had promised the newspapers that he would beat everyone to a cheap, practical electric light. His name was Thomas Edison, and his team was working day and night.

deepDive: Why does Swan's name come first in Britain and Edison's in America? Part of the answer is national pride, but part is genuinely technical. Historians usually separate three things: who first made a carbon lamp glow in a vacuum, who first made one that lasted long enough to sell, and who first built a system to supply many lamps cheaply. Swan had a glowing carbonised-paper lamp by about 1860, decades before Edison, but it was not practical. His December 1878 and February 1879 demonstrations came before Edison's successful carbon-filament test of 22 October 1879, which is why British courts took his priority seriously. However, Swan's early lamps used comparatively thick carbon rods with low resistance. The power P drawn by a lamp equals V times I (voltage times current). For the same light, a low-resistance lamp needs a large current at a low voltage, and the power wasted in the supply wires is I squared times R, so doubling the current roughly quadruples the loss. That forces either very thick copper mains or lamps wired in series, where one failure darkens the whole chain. Edison's team, guided by Francis Upton's calculations, deliberately chased a high-resistance filament (around 100 ohms or more when hot) so lamps could be wired in parallel at about 100 volts with modest currents. Swan's parchmentised cotton thread (patent 1880) and his squirted nitrocellulose filaments (patented 1881) moved his lamp toward that ideal. The squirted-cellulose method was so good that it later became the standard way of making carbon filaments, and the same principle fed into the artificial-fibre industry. Another debate concerns vacuum technology: Swan is said to have described a mercury pump in 1863, but the Sprengel pump of 1865 was the one that spread through laboratories, and Swan's later success depended on Charles Stearn's skill with it, especially the trick of heating the filament while pumping to drive out trapped gases. The 1883 Ediswan merger was a business compromise rather than a court verdict on who invented the bulb. The fairest summary is that the practical incandescent lamp was a shared, overlapping achievement, and Swan's Newcastle work was an essential part of it.
funFact: When Richard D'Oyly Carte wanted to prove his new electric lights were safe, he broke a glowing bulb on the Savoy Theatre stage in front of the audience, and nothing caught fire.
